children: CEO Sam Altman said his company remains fundamentally divided with rival Anthropic
over how aggressively artificial intelligence should be regulated, arguing that society should tolerate some harms in exchange for the technology's broader benefits and widespread availability.
In an interview with Politico's Decoded, Altman said OpenAI
favors giving individuals broad access to powerful AI rather than concentrating control among a small number of developers.
“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman said.
The comments highlight a philosophical difference between two of the leading developers of frontier AI. Anthropic

, led by CEO Dario Amodei, has generally advocated stronger safeguards for the most advanced models, while OpenAI has favored a lighter regulatory approach. Altman rejected the idea that eliminating misuse would justify tightly restricting access, arguing that AI's beneficial uses ultimately will vastly outweigh harmful ones.

The gap between the companies has narrowed, however. OpenAI recently supported state laws imposing tougher safety requirements, backed a bipartisan House proposal for independent evaluations of advanced models and agreed with Amodei's call to slow development of the most capable AI systems. Those moves followed security incidents involving increasingly autonomous AI models.

Altman nevertheless argued against an approach in which a handful of companies effectively control access to advanced AI because of safety concerns. At the same time, he drew a distinction between tolerable misuse and potentially catastrophic outcomes, saying he doesn't accept risks involving “a serious loss of control to AI.”

The debate has potentially significant consequences for OpenAI, Anthropic and the broader AI industry. Rules governing model safety, independent testing and access could raise development costs and affect how quickly new systems reach customers. They also could influence competition if compliance requirements are expensive enough to favor well-funded incumbents over startups. OpenAI's evolving position suggests regulation is becoming a more important consideration as AI models gain greater autonomy.

Anthropic pushed back against suggestions that its preferred regulations would entrench the largest developers. A company spokesperson said its proposals apply only to frontier models. Amodei has previously argued that Anthropic deliberately favors policies that impose greater burdens on leading AI companies while giving smaller competitors more room to develop.

The dispute is emerging as Washington intensifies its focus on AI safety while trying to preserve U.S. leadership in the technology. The central policy question increasingly isn't whether advanced AI requires safeguards, but how much risk governments should tolerate before restrictions begin to outweigh the economic and technological benefits.

title: OpenAI’s Altman draws regulatory divide with Anthropic over AI risks: Politico
